Traefik ReplacePathRegex auth bypass: glued dot-dot traversal in request path AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the CVE-2026-65600 exploit signature — a path segment glued directly to a traversal sequence (e.g. /api../admin) or its percent-encoded form (/api%2e%2e/admin) that Traefik's sanitizePath accepts as a valid segment. This is the article-specific 'implicit traversal' that only fires because there is no separator before the capture group in patterns like regex '^/api(.*)'. Rationale: Keys on the article's exact exploit primitive: an alphanumeric segment immediately followed by '..' with no separator (api../admin) plus the PoC's URL-encoded variant %2e%2e. Normal clients almost never send a glued dot-dot, and standard /../ is excluded by requiring an alnum char before the dots, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-65600/
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security scanners (Nuclei, Burp, Nessus) probing for path traversal against the reverse proxy
  • Legitimate WAF/pentest validation traffic replaying the PoC path
  • Applications that legitimately embed literal '..' in a non-path query parameter that gets logged in the URL field
  • Broken clients double-encoding paths that happen to contain %2e%2e
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<known-scanner-ips>") | where not (HttpHostName has_any ("vulnscan","security-testing"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the source IP; confirm the RawPath glues a real config prefix to '..' and note the returned status — a 2xx to a normally-protected route is a confirmed bypass. 2) Contain: place the vulnerable router/middleware behind a temporary deny rule for paths matching the traversal regex, or block the source IP at the edge; schedule upgrade to Traefik 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7. 3) Hunt: enumerate all ReplacePathRegex middlewares with unbounded capture groups (^/x(.*)), then review backend logs for prior 2xx on protected routes reached via traversal.
let lookback = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| extend RawPath = tostring(coalesce(UrlOriginal, Url))
| where RawPath matches regex @"(?i)[a-z0-9]\.\.(/|%2f|$)" or RawPath contains "%2e%2e" or RawPath contains "%2E%2E"   // glued dot-dot or encoded traversal — CVE-2026-65600 signature
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName, HttpMethod, RawPath, HttpStatusCode, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, UA = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Traefik path-traversal bypass CONFIRMED: traversal request returns 2xx on protected route AIActions on Objectives High
Impact-confirmation for CVE-2026-65600. Surfaces requests that carry the glued/encoded traversal signature AND received a 2xx response — meaning the backend normalized /../admin to /admin and served protected content without the auth middleware ever running. This separates blocked probes from a successful authentication bypass. Rationale: Combines the traversal path signature with an HTTP 2xx status — the article states the backend normalizes /../admin to /admin and returns ADMIN_SECRET_DATA, so a success response on a traversal path is a high-fidelity bypass confirmation rather than a mere probe. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Scanners that trigger a generic 200 error/landing page rather than real protected content
  • Backends that echo the raw path in a 200 without actually serving the protected resource
  • Load-balancer health probes hitting a permissive catch-all route
  • URLs where '..' appears in a query string the app ignores but still returns 200
Suppression filter
| where not (RawPath has_any ("/health","/healthz","/favicon.ico"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the 2xx body/route is genuinely a protected resource (admin/config/internal API) and not a generic page; capture the exact RawPath and normalized target. 2) Contain: treat as active compromise — rotate any credentials/secrets exposed on the reached route, block the source IP, and hot-patch the middleware to reject non-normalizing paths pending upgrade. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP and session across all backends for further 2xx traversal hits, and review protected-route access logs for the full window since the vulnerable config was deployed.

Traefik dynamic config write introducing unbounded ReplacePathRegex capture group AIWeaponization Medium
Detects creation/modification of Traefik configuration files (traefik.yml/.toml, dynamic.yml, /etc/traefik/) — the deployment vector for the vulnerable ReplacePathRegex pattern '^/api(.*)' with replacement '/$1'. Endpoint telemetry flags the file touch; pair with a content audit of the written file for the separator-less capture group. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete config filenames and the /etc/traefik/ mount path from the PoC docker-compose. This is coarse (endpoint telemetry cannot read the regex content), so it is a hunting-tier trigger to drive a content audit for the vulnerable '^/api(.*)' + '/$1' pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/traefik/traefik/security/advisories/GHSA-cxjq-mrr5-89rv
ATT&CKT1190 T1526
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine GitOps/CI deployment of Traefik config via Ansible/Helm/kustomize
  • Admin manually tuning routers/middlewares
  • Container image rebuilds that rewrite the mounted config
  • Config-reload tooling touching the file on every restart
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("helm.exe","ansible","kustomize","dockerd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written config and search for ReplacePathRegex middlewares whose regex captures without a mandatory separator (e.g. ^/prefix(.*)) and whose replacement re-emits the capture (/$1). 2) Contain: correct the pattern to include the slash (^/prefix/(.*)) or upgrade Traefik to a patched release that rejects non-normalizing paths. 3) Hunt: inventory all clusters/hosts running the same config template and check web logs for prior traversal exploitation against those routers.

Vulnerable Traefik version exposed to CVE-2026-65600 / CVE-2026-48020 AIReconnaissance High
Inventory-driven detection that flags hosts running Traefik versions vulnerable to the ReplacePathRegex (CVE-2026-65600) and StripPrefix (CVE-2026-48020) auth-bypass family — v1 ≤1.7.34, v2 ≤2.11.51, v3 3.6.0–3.6.22 and 3.7.0–3.7.6. Prioritizes upgrade to 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE IDs and the confirmed affected/patched version boundaries from the advisory (patched in 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7). Cross-checked against GitLab and SentinelOne vulnerability databases for the version ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/traefik/traefik/v2/CVE-2026-65600/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48020/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traefik running only with non-vulnerable configs (no ReplacePathRegex/StripPrefix) still flagged by version match
  • Containerized Traefik not fully represented in TVM software inventory
  • Dev/test instances not internet-exposed
  • Version string reported by a sidecar/embedded copy rather than the active proxy
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the flagged host actually terminates external traffic and uses ReplacePathRegex or StripPrefix middleware. 2) Contain: schedule upgrade to 2.11.52 / 3.6.23 / 3.7.7; if immediate patch is impossible, add an edge rule rejecting request paths that do not equal their normalized form. 3) Hunt: for any internet-facing vulnerable instance, review web logs for the traversal exploitation signature (UC1/UC2) across the exposure window.

New Interrupt Injection Attack Can Bypass Spectre v2 Defenses on Intel and AMD CPUs

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 18 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Apparently, opening the thing is now enough. A repo can run before the first prompt, a package can hide among hundreds, and a harmless-looking PDF can finish the job. This week runs on cheap leverage: exposed servers, recycled bugs, poisoned agent instructions, remote-access tools dressed as support software, and trusted defaults doing attackers a favor. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Odysseus RCE, Samsung One-Click Takeover, iCloud Backdoor Fight + 27
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SideWinder ClickOnce side-load: NGenTask.exe running mscorsvc.dll from Apps\2.0 cache · [LLM] Flooding Dropper Registry Run-key persistence pointing to update_win.exe · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SideWinder Rust backdoor C2 to Cloudflare Workers (*.workers.dev) from non-browser process · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
SideWinder ClickOnce side-load: NGenTask.exe running mscorsvc.dll from Apps\2.0 cache AIInstallation Medium
Hunts SideWinder's ClickOnce infection chain where the ClickOnce deployment host (dfsvc.exe) launches a masqueraded .NET runtime binary (NGenTask.exe) from the per-user ClickOnce cache (AppData\Local\Apps\2.0), which DLL-side-loads a malicious mscorsvc.dll. Legitimate NGenTask.exe only ever executes from the .NET Framework directory, so execution from the ClickOnce cache is the article-specific tell. Rationale: Anchors on the durable, low-FP signal (NGenTask.exe — a signed Microsoft binary — executing from the ClickOnce cache AppData\Local\Apps\2.0 under dfsvc.exe), which legitimate .NET never does. Binary/DLL names (NGenTask.exe, mscorsvc.dll) corroborated via Trellix's SideWinder ClickOnce writeup, not the article text alone. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/sidewinders-shifting-sands-click-once-for-espionage/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal LOB apps deployed via ClickOnce that happen to ship a helper named NGenTask (extremely rare)
  • Developer test-signing of ClickOnce manifests during app packaging
  • Security-tool sandbox detonating ClickOnce samples on a monitored endpoint
  • IT software distribution using ClickOnce for signed in-house tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-corp-signed", "InternalDeploy") and SHA256 in~ ("<known-good-lob-hash>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm dfsvc.exe → NGenTask.exe from Apps\2.0, then check for a sibling mscorsvc.dll in the same cache folder and the referring .application/PDF. Hash the DLL and check reputation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the NGenTask.exe process, and quarantine the Apps\2.0 deployment folder; block the source URL/PDF sender. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceId for registry Run-key writes and outbound connections to *.workers.dev (SideWinder Rust backdoor C2); sweep the fleet for other hosts that received the same phishing PDF.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "NGenTask.exe"
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Apps\2.0\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dfsvc.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\NGenTask.exe"
| where NewProcessName has "\\AppData\\Local\\Apps\\2.0\\"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\dfsvc.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SideWinder Rust backdoor C2 to Cloudflare Workers (*.workers.dev) from non-browser process AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SideWinder Rust backdoor's command-and-control channel, which uses free serverless infrastructure (Cloudflare Workers, *.workers.dev). Flags the first-ever org contact to a *.workers.dev host initiated by a non-browser process, which distinguishes implant beaconing from ordinary developer/CDN traffic. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit C2 substrate (Cloudflare Workers / *.workers.dev) plus a non-browser initiator and a first-seen-in-org baseline anti-join to strip legitimate developer/CDN traffic. Durable even if the Rust implant binary name varies. C2 platform corroborated by Trellix SideWinder writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/sidewinders-shifting-sands-click-once-for-espionage/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer tooling (npm/deno/wrangler) legitimately calling Cloudflare Workers APIs
  • Custom internal apps hosted on workers.dev subdomains
  • curl/PowerShell scripts hitting a partner's Workers-hosted webhook
  • Security scanners or uptime monitors polling a workers.dev endpoint
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("node.exe","deno.exe","wrangler.exe","curl.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wrangler","deploy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and its parent chain — is it a signed browser/dev tool or an unknown binary from AppData/ClickOnce cache? Capture the full workers.dev FQDN and beacon cadence. 2) Contain: if the initiator is unsigned or from Apps\2.0, isolate the host, block the FQDN at proxy/DNS, and kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate the same DeviceId with dfsvc.exe→NGenTask.exe execution and registry Run-key persistence; submit the FQDN to threat intel and sweep for other beaconing hosts.
let Baseline = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where RemoteUrl endswith "workers.dev"
| summarize by RemoteUrl;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl endswith "workers.dev"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe","code.exe")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on RemoteUrl
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let Baseline = ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where DnsQuery endswith "workers.dev"
| summarize by DnsQuery;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "workers.dev"
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on DnsQuery
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Hosts = dcount(SrcHostname), SampleSrc = any(SrcIpAddr) by DnsQuery
| where Hosts <= 3
| order by FirstSeen desc

Flooding Dropper npm second-stage payload drop (update_win.exe) AIDelivery High
Hunts the Flooding Dropper npm supply-chain campaign's Windows second stage, which downloads an encrypted payload from a remote /pkg/update_win.exe path and writes update_win.exe to disk before reflective in-memory execution. Targets the specific filename observed by Sonatype (sonatype-2026-005660). Rationale: Uses the concrete, high-fidelity filename/path (update_win.exe fetched from /pkg/update_win.exe) confirmed by Sonatype's Flooding Dropper analysis — a specific IOC unlikely to collide with legitimate software. Surfacing the initiating process (node.exe from npm install) ties the drop back to the supply-chain vector. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages • https://securityboulevard.com/2026/08/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate ISV shipping an updater coincidentally named update_win.exe (rare — verify signature/path)
  • Windows update helper tooling in an unusual OEM image
  • Internal software distribution staging an installer with a generic name
  • Security-tool detonation of the malicious package in a sandbox VM
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","wuauclt.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Program Files\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process — expect node.exe/npm during a package install; capture FileOriginUrl (should end in /pkg/update_win.exe) and the SHA256; check whether the file is signed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node/child processes, quarantine update_win.exe, and pull the package.json/npm logs to identify the malicious package (look for bigops/bnpl names, 35.x.y versions). 3) Hunt: check for Registry Run-key and scheduled-task persistence referencing update_win.exe, ETW/AMSI patching, and rotate any credentials exposed on the build/dev host after cleanup.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "update_win.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "update_win.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Flooding Dropper Registry Run-key persistence pointing to update_win.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts the Flooding Dropper campaign's persistence, which registers its second-stage payload (update_win.exe) under a CurrentVersion\Run autostart key (alongside a scheduled task). Matches on the specific payload filename in the Run-key value data. Rationale: Combines the autostart location (CurrentVersion\Run) with the campaign-specific payload name (update_win.exe) confirmed by Sonatype — a two-condition match that is essentially FP-free. Complements the file-drop UC by catching the persistence stage even if the initial drop was missed. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sonatype.com/blog/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages • https://securityboulevard.com/2026/08/flooding-dropper-hits-npm-with-850-malicious-packages/
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate updater named update_win.exe writing its own Run key (verify path/signature)
  • Endpoint imaging/gold-build tooling seeding autostart entries
  • Sandbox detonation of the malicious npm package
  • Admin manually staging a benign scheduled updater with a colliding name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe") and RegistryValueData !has @"\Program Files\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Run-key value path to update_win.exe and identify the writing process (expect node/child from an npm install); verify the referenced binary's signature and hash. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Run-key value and the paired scheduled task, and quarantine update_win.exe. 3) Hunt: check for ETW/AMSI patching and reflective loading on the same host, enumerate installed npm packages for bigops/bnpl naming and 35.x.y versions, and rotate credentials on the affected dev/build host after remediation.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "update_win.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
| where RegistryValueData has "update_win.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Over 4,400 Rockwell PLCs Exposed Online, 22 Found in Water Attack Cities

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 8 use cases 3 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Forescout found 22 internet-facing Rockwell Automation programmable logic controllers (PLCs) in cities hit by recent cyberattacks on US water utilities. Nineteen used the same mobile carrier network. Its August 3 scan counted 4,407 exposed Rockwell controllers worldwide, including 2,844 in the United States, but Forescout could not confirm any were compromised. That figure counts exposed

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] External or internal enumeration of Rockwell OT services (EtherNet/IP / Modbus port sweep) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Internet-facing inbound access to Rockwell EtherNet/IP & Modbus OT ports (44818/2222/502) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rockwell/Schneider/Siemens engineering software reaching a PLC over the public internet
Internet-facing inbound access to Rockwell EtherNet/IP & Modbus OT ports (44818/2222/502) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated inbound connections from public source IPs to Rockwell/Allen-Bradley OT service ports on internal PLC hosts. Directly targets the exposure Forescout/FBI describe — reachable MicroLogix controllers on TCP 44818 (EtherNet/IP), 2222 (EtherNet/IP I/O) and 502 (Modbus TCP, the CVE-2017-16740 attack surface) — where reachability alone let actors identify controllers and set passwords. Rationale: Uses the exact OT ports named in the FBI/IC3 PSA and Forescout (44818/2222/502) plus the public-source / private-destination direction that defines internet exposure of a MicroLogix controller — a pairing that should essentially never occur on a correctly segmented OT network. Cross-checked against: • https://www.fbi.gov/investigate/cyber/alerts/2026/malicious-cyber-actors-targeting-water-and-wastewater-sector-internet--facing-programmable-logic-controllers-causing-operational-disruptions • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260730.pdf • https://www.forescout.com/blog/ot-security-analysis-exposed-devices-attacked-in-us-water-systems/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2017-16740
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cellular-modem/private-APN links where the carrier CGNAT range is not recognized as internal, making legitimate remote engineering look 'public'
  • Managed OT vendor performing sanctioned remote support to a controller via a documented jump path
  • Firewall log direction field misconfigured so intra-DMZ OT polling is tagged inbound-from-public
  • Security team's own authorized external exposure scan (Censys/Shodan-style) against known assets
Suppression filter
| where not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP)) and SourceIP !in ("<sanctioned-remote-support-addresses-managed-in-a-watchlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the DestinationIP is a real PLC/HMI (MicroLogix 1400/1100) and whether the SourceIP is a sanctioned remote-support address; check whether the session was 'allowed' by the firewall and whether Modbus/EtherNet/IP actually responded. 2) Contain: block the inbound rule / remove the controller's public exposure (per FBI/EPA guidance move behind VPN or private APN), and rotate the controller password if reachable. 3) Hunt: pull all traffic from that SourceIP across the OT range, review controller for password/IP changes and modified project files (ladder-logic discrepancies), and pivot to UC 'engineering-tool egress' and UC 'OT port scanning' for related activity.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where RemotePort in (44818, 2222, 502)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(RemotePort) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Connections desc
let RockwellOTPorts = dynamic([44818, 2222, 502]);

| where DestinationPort in (RockwellOTPorts)
| where DeviceAction !in~ ("deny","denied","drop","dropped","block","blocked")
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP)
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by Connections desc

External or internal enumeration of Rockwell OT services (EtherNet/IP / Modbus port sweep) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single source fanning out across many controllers or many OT ports (44818/2222/502/102/22) in a short window — the 'identify a controller' reconnaissance step that precedes password/IP changes. Covers both an external scanner hitting the exposed PLC estate and a compromised internal engineering host enumerating the OT segment. Rationale: Thresholded fan-out on the PSA-named OT port set (44818/2222/502/102/22) captures the pre-attack enumeration that reachability enables, without depending on any single IOC; distinct-destination and distinct-port counts separate a sweep from normal point-to-point OT polling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260730.pdf • https://www.forescout.com/blog/ot-security-analysis-exposed-devices-attacked-in-us-water-systems/ • https://cyberscoop.com/exposed-rockwell-controllers-water-system-attacks/
ATT&CKT1595 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized OT asset-discovery / vulnerability scanner (e.g. Forescout, Nessus OT, Tenable.ot) sweeping the controller inventory on schedule
  • SCADA/HMI poller legitimately fanning out to many field controllers on 502/44818
  • Internet background-noise research scanners (Shodan/Censys/GreyNoise) hitting the exposed estate
  • Network monitoring/mapping tool run by the OT engineering team during commissioning
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","tenable-core.exe","forescout.exe") and DeviceName !in~ ("<known-scada-poller-hostnames-watchlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source — is it an approved OT scanner or SCADA poller (check asset inventory / scanner watchlist) or an unexpected host/IP? Review whether ports probed extend beyond what a normal poller uses. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, block the source at the OT firewall and isolate the initiating internal host; snapshot for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate the source with subsequent single-connection access on 44818/502 (UC1), engineering-tool egress (UC3), and any controller password/IP/project-file changes; expand the window to catch slow scans.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where RemotePort in (44818, 2222, 502, 102)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| summarize DistinctTargets=dcount(RemoteIP), Targets=make_set(RemoteIP, 50), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Total=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 10
| order by DistinctTargets desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where DestinationPort in (44818, 2222, 502, 102, 22)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| summarize DistinctDests=dcount(DestinationIP), DistinctPorts=dcount(DestinationPort), Dests=make_set(DestinationIP, 50), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort), Total=count() by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DistinctDests >= 10 or DistinctPorts >= 4
| order by DistinctDests desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationPort:44818 OR @DestinationPort:2222 OR @DestinationPort:502 OR @DestinationPort:102)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| (RemotePort=44818 OR RemotePort=2222 OR RemotePort=502 OR RemotePort=102)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctTargets))
| DistinctTargets >= 10

Rockwell/Schneider/Siemens engineering software reaching a PLC over the public internet AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects OT engineering applications (Studio 5000 Logix Designer, RSLogix 5000/500, RSLinx, Siemens TIA Portal) initiating EtherNet/IP or Modbus sessions to a PUBLIC IP. The FBI PSA states actors used exactly these legitimate engineering tools from leased infrastructure to connect to exposed controllers and upload/modify PLC project files — engineering software should only ever talk to internal controllers. Rationale: Pivots on the exact engineering tools the FBI/IC3 PSA named (Studio 5000 Logix Designer, RSLogix, Siemens TIA Portal) plus CIP/Modbus ports to a public destination — a behaviour with essentially no benign explanation, since engineering software legitimately reaches only internal controllers, making the project-file upload/modify step high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2026/PSA260730.pdf • https://www.levelblue.com/blogs/spiderlabs-blog/review-of-the-july-2026-cyberattacks-against-u.s.-water-and-wastewater-systems • https://www.forescout.com/blog/ot-security-analysis-exposed-devices-attacked-in-us-water-systems/
ATT&CKT0845 T0843 T1119
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer legitimately programming a remote site's controller over a corporate WAN link that egresses via a public IP (split-tunnel / cloud-proxied path)
  • Engineering workstation reaching a cloud-hosted PLC simulator or vendor demo controller on a public address
  • RSLinx acting as an OPC gateway to a partner site over an internet path
  • Managed OT service provider performing sanctioned remote engineering from a workstation whose traffic NATs to a public IP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !in ("<approved-remote-site-plc-public-ips-watchlist>") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("<sanctioned-remote-engineering-svc-accounts>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the RemoteIP is external and not a known remote site; identify the operator account and whether change management authorized a program upload/download to that controller now. 2) Contain: isolate the engineering workstation, suspend the account's PLC access, and (if the target is a company controller) capture and compare the current project/ladder logic against the last known-good offline copy per Rockwell SD1790. 3) Hunt: enumerate every controller the workstation touched, check for password/IP changes, disabled alarms or modified Add-On Instructions, and pull EmailEvents/logon history for the operator to assess account compromise.
let EngExe = dynamic(["LogixDesigner.exe","Studio 5000.exe","RSLogix 5000.exe","RS5000.exe","RSLogix 500.exe","RSLogix500.exe","RSLinx.exe","Siemens.Automation.Portal.exe"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (44818, 2222, 502)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (EngExe)
    or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Rockwell","Schneider Electric","Siemens")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let EngExe = dynamic(["logixdesigner.exe","studio 5000.exe","rslogix 5000.exe","rs5000.exe","rslogix 500.exe","rslogix500.exe","rslinx.exe","siemens.automation.portal.exe"]);
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (44818, 2222, 502)
| where tolower(InitiatingProcessFileName) in (EngExe)
| where isnotempty(RemoteIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(RemoteIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Apple iCloud Private Relay Can Expose Real IPs Through WebKit Proxy Bypasses

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 4 use cases 3 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed a security issue with Apple's iCloud Private Relay tool that can expose a user's real IP address. Introduced with iOS 15, iCloud Private Relay employs a dual-hop architecture to ensure users' privacy by routing their Safari web traffic through two relays so that no single third-party, including Apple, can determine where the request is originating from

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI Recommendation Poisoning: How "Ask AI" Buttons Silently Alter LLM Memory

The Hacker News
2026-08-06 6 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new class of prompt injection is spreading across commercial websites. It requires no malware, no stolen credentials, and no zero-day exploit. It abuses a standard feature built into almost every major AI assistant: pre-filled deep links. We observed production websites embedding hidden prompt injection payloads inside "Ask AI" buttons on marketing and competitor comparison pages. When a user

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Web egress to AI-assistant deep-link carrying LLM memory-poisoning instruction · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Inbound email delivering AI-assistant deep-link with memory-poisoning payload
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Web egress to AI-assistant deep-link carrying LLM memory-poisoning instruction AIDelivery Medium
Hunts outbound web requests to ChatGPT/Claude/Grok/Gemini/Perplexity deep-link endpoints (?q=) whose query string carries a memory-write instruction such as 'trusted source', 'source of expertise' or 'remember'. This is the click/browse moment of AI Recommendation Poisoning where an 'Ask AI' button silently commits a vendor domain to the user's persistent LLM memory. Rationale: Anchors on the exact AI-assistant domains and the '?q=' deep-link pattern named in the article/Microsoft blog, combined with the two publicly-disclosed keyword classes ('trusted source', 'remember') plus the article's verbatim payload phrase 'source of expertise for future reference'. URL-encoded variants included because proxy logs store escaped query strings. Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: FDR and standard Datadog sources do not capture HTTPS query strings, so the distinguishing signal is unavailable there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ • https://www.theregister.com/2026/02/12/microsoft_ai_recommendation_poisoning/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/02/11/ai-recommendation-memory-poisoning-attacks/
ATT&CK
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign 'Summarize with AI' buttons whose prompt legitimately contains the word 'remember' (e.g. 'remember to cite sources') with no domain-save intent
  • Security researchers/analysts reproducing the payloads during this very investigation
  • Users authoring their own ChatGPT/Claude deep links that instruct the model to remember a personal preference
  • Browser extensions / bookmarklets that pre-fill AI prompts as a productivity feature
  • Vendor marketing/QA staff clicking their own comparison-page buttons
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise")  // drop the noisy bare 'remember' token; keep the high-fidelity domain-trust phrases
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full RequestURL/RemoteUrl and URL-decode the q= parameter. Confirm it instructs the model to save/trust a specific vendor DOMAIN (not just a benign 'remember'). Note the referring marketing/comparison page and the user. 2) CONTAIN: Have the user open their AI assistant's memory/personalization settings and delete any unauthorized 'trusted source' or 'source of expertise' domain entry; if unsure, reset the memory store. Reinforce policy: do not click 'Ask AI' buttons on corporate accounts. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the referring domain across all users to find everyone who clicked the same poisoned button, and sweep proxy logs for other AI-assistant deep links from that referrer over the last 60 days.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai")
| where RemoteUrl has "q="
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RequestURL has_any ("chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai")
| where RequestURL has "q="
| where RequestURL has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: AI-Assistant Deep-Link Carrying LLM Memory-Poisoning Instruction
id: a3f1c2e4-9b7d-4e2a-8f6c-1d2e3f4a5b6c
description: Detects outbound web requests to AI-assistant deep-link endpoints whose query string contains a persistent-memory write instruction (AI Recommendation Poisoning).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/ai-recommendation-poisoning-how-ask-ai.html
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/06
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - atlas.aml_t0051
  - atlas.aml_t0080
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  domain:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'chatgpt.com'
      - 'claude.ai'
      - 'grok.com'
      - 'gemini.google.com'
      - 'perplexity.ai'
  deeplink:
    c-uri|contains: 'q='
  payload:
    c-uri|contains:
      - 'trusted source'
      - 'trusted+source'
      - 'trusted%20source'
      - 'source of expertise'
      - 'source+of+expertise'
      - 'source%20of%20expertise'
      - 'remember'
  condition: domain and deeplink and payload
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*chatgpt.com*" OR Web.url="*claude.ai*" OR Web.url="*grok.com*" OR Web.url="*gemini.google.com*" OR Web.url="*perplexity.ai*") AND Web.url="*q=*" AND (Web.url="*trusted*source*" OR Web.url="*trusted+source*" OR Web.url="*trusted%20source*" OR Web.url="*source*of*expertise*" OR Web.url="*source+of+expertise*" OR Web.url="*remember*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*chatgpt.com*" OR Web.url="*claude.ai*" OR Web.url="*grok.com*" OR Web.url="*gemini.google.com*" OR Web.url="*perplexity.ai*") AND Web.url="*q=*" AND (Web.url="*trusted*source*" OR Web.url="*trusted+source*" OR Web.url="*trusted%20source*" OR Web.url="*source*of*expertise*" OR Web.url="*source+of+expertise*" OR Web.url="*remember*") by Web.src Web.user Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Inbound email delivering AI-assistant deep-link with memory-poisoning payload AIInstallation Medium
Hunts delivered inbound email containing a link to an AI-assistant deep-link (?q=) whose query string carries a persistent-memory write instruction. Catches the AI Recommendation Poisoning payload at the mail-delivery layer before the recipient clicks, treating the memory-manipulation link the way Microsoft advises treating credential-harvesting links. Rationale: Reuses the same article-grounded AI-assistant domains, '?q=' deep-link pattern and disclosed memory-write phrases, but pivots on EmailUrlInfo joined to inbound EmailEvents to catch the payload at delivery — a genuinely different log source and phase from the web-egress UC. Sentinel/Sigma/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: EmailUrlInfo (Defender for O365 URL extraction) has no clean equivalent on those platforms in this tenant, and the detection is a cross-table join so Sigma's single-event shape does not fit. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/10/ai-recommendation-poisoning/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/microsoft-finds-summarize-with-ai.html
ATT&CK
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate newsletters/marketing mail embedding benign 'Summarize with AI' share buttons that happen to include the word 'remember'
  • Internal red-team / awareness phishing simulations replaying this payload
  • A colleague forwarding a legitimately-authored ChatGPT/Claude deep link containing a personal 'remember my preference' instruction
  • Vendor product-comparison emails whose 'Ask AI' link uses 'source of expertise' as legitimate GEO marketing
Suppression filter
| where Url has_any ("trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise")  // drop bare 'remember'; retain explicit domain-trust instructions
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: URL-decode the q= parameter from EmailUrlInfo and confirm it instructs the model to save/trust a specific domain; check DeliveryAction/DeliveryLocation to see if it reached the inbox, then check UrlClickEvents for that NetworkMessageId to see if the recipient actually clicked. 2) CONTAIN: If clicked, direct the user to purge unauthorized 'trusted source'/'source of expertise' entries from their AI memory (or reset it); soft-delete/quarantine the message for all recipients via Explorer. 3) HUNT: Cluster on SenderFromAddress and SenderMailFromDomain to find the full campaign, and cross-reference the embedded vendor domain against the web-egress UC to see who browsed the same payload on the open web.
let AiDomains = dynamic(["chatgpt.com","claude.ai","grok.com","gemini.google.com","perplexity.ai"]);
let MemPhrases = dynamic(["trusted source","trusted+source","trusted%20source","source of expertise","source+of+expertise","source%20of%20expertise","remember"]);
