OVSwrap AppArmor bypass: `aa-exec -p trinity` userns-restriction fallback (Ubuntu 24.04) AIExploitation High
Detects the OVSwrap PoC's AppArmor bypass fallback — where direct namespace creation is blocked on Ubuntu 24.04, the exploit re-runs itself under the permissive `trinity` profile via `aa-exec -p trinity` to restore reachability to the vulnerable path. The `aa-exec -p trinity` string is a near-unique PoC artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact PoC artifact `aa-exec -p trinity`, an AppArmor-confinement bypass specific to the OVSwrap exploit on Ubuntu 24.04 — extremely unlikely to appear in benign administration. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://pbxscience.com/ovswrap-flaw-in-linux-kernels-open-vswitch-lets-local-users-become-root/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site that legitimately ships a custom AppArmor profile literally named 'trinity'
  • Security researchers reproducing the OVSwrap PoC in an authorized lab
  • AppArmor profile testing/QA that invokes aa-exec with a named profile
  • Automated exploit-detection or vuln-scanning tooling replaying the PoC
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is near-unique to the PoC — immediately confirm the host, actor, and whether a 'trinity' AppArmor profile even legitimately exists there (`aa-status`). 2) Contain: isolate the host, freeze the invoking account, capture memory/process tree; on Ubuntu re-enable the userns AppArmor restriction and apply the openvswitch module block. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the full chain — preceding `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, and following /etc/sudoers* modification or unexpected uid=0 shells.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "aa-exec"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "trinity"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/aa-exec" or TargetProcessName == "aa-exec"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "trinity" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","--profile")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OVSwrap post-exploit: /etc/sudoers or /etc/sudoers.d modified outside package/config tooling AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the OVSwrap PoC's post-root action — after corrupting a kernel credential it modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to entrench root access before opening a root shell. Flags writes to these paths by processes that are not the sanctioned sudoers editors or package/config-management tooling. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit post-exploit action — the PoC modifies /etc/sudoers.d or /etc/sudoers to persist root — and filters the known-good editors/package managers so only anomalous writers surface. Datadog left empty: the linux.auditd standard schema exposes process/user fields but not a reliable file-path attribute for this write. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/new-ovswrap-linux-kernel-flaw-lets.html • https://blog.cloudlinux.com/ovswrap-cve-2026-64531-mitigation/
ATT&CKT1548.003 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying sudoers drop-ins
  • cloud-init seeding sudoers for a new cloud instance's default user
  • Admin adding a sudo rule via a text editor instead of visudo
  • Package post-install scripts dropping files into /etc/sudoers.d
  • IdM/SSSD or FreeIPA tooling syncing sudo rules
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("salt-minion","ansible","puppet","chef-client","cloud-init")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the newly written sudoers content and identify the writing process and user — a non-editor writer (e.g. an exploit binary or unexpected shell) adding NOPASSWD/ALL for a normal user is high-confidence malicious. 2) Contain: revert the sudoers change, revoke/reset the affected account, isolate the host and preserve the file plus process tree for forensics. 3) Hunt: correlate on the same host for the OVSwrap precursors — `unshare -Urn`, openvswitch module load, `aa-exec -p trinity` — and any root shell spawned immediately after the write; patch to a fixed vendor kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath == "/etc/sudoers" or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init","unattended-upgr")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath == "/etc/sudoers" or TargetFilePath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileWrite")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("visudo","sudoedit","apt","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","puppet","chef-client","ansible","cloud-init"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",

     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:

detection:

Kali365 Weaponizes Microsoft Authentication Against US Companies: New Enterprise Risk

The Hacker News
2026-08-05 9 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Kali365 is turning a legitimate Microsoft login into a gateway to corporate data. The phishing kit targets US organizations with attacker-controlled device codes that victims approve on Microsoft's real authentication page. Once access and refresh tokens are issued, attackers may retain access to email, documents, and cloud resources, creating a direct path to data exposure, financial fraud,

ATT&CKT1190 T1528 T1566 T1566.002
Domainsbluefoodtruths.xyz flexiscalesystems.de guardedwebsolutions.de proforcstaffing.com reputationboosters.de guardextion.online prowebsitemakers.de onlinebrandinghub.de onsite-developments.net functionalityfirst.de

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Kali365 device-code-flow authentication used by a standard M365 user AIExploitation Medium
Hunts successful Entra ID sign-ins that completed via the OAuth device-code grant, which Kali365 abuses to have victims approve an attacker-generated code on Microsoft's real login page. Device-code flow is legitimate but rare for interactive knowledge workers, making its appearance on a normal user account a high-value pivot for token theft. Rationale: Uses the article's core TTP — attacker-controlled device codes approved on Microsoft's legitimate device-login portal — expressed as the OAuth device-code grant, which is the single defining signal of Kali365 token issuance. AuthenticationProtocol not being an available column in this tenant's SigninLogs schema, the flow is matched on the deviceCode marker inside AuthenticationDetails. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1621/
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineers authenticating Azure CLI / Azure PowerShell on a shell that cannot pop a browser
  • Conference-room / Teams Rooms and smart-TV devices enrolling via device code
  • IoT or headless kiosk provisioning that legitimately uses the device-code grant
  • Developers logging into az login --use-device-code over SSH
  • New MDM/Intune device onboarding using device-code sign-in
Suppression filter
| where not (Application has_any ("Microsoft Azure CLI","Microsoft Azure PowerShell") and DeviceTrustType == "Azure AD joined")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the user's device-code sign-ins — check the resource/app requested, source IP geo, and whether the user owns a headless/CLI workflow that would explain it. Compare the sign-in IP to the user's normal locations. 2. Contain: if unexplained, revoke the user's refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession / 'Revoke sessions'), force password reset, and require re-MFA; block the source IP. 3. Hunt: enumerate all OAuth tokens/apps consented for the account, review mailbox rules and recent mail/file access, and search other users for device-code sign-ins from the same IP/ASN within 24h.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in the auth-detail JSON
| where ErrorCode == 0                            // completed sign-in => token issued
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(Country, 20),
            Apps = make_set(Application, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by AccountUpn, AccountDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"   // device-code grant marker in AuthenticationDetails JSON
| where ResultType == 0                           // successful sign-in
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20), Countries = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            Apps = make_set(AppDisplayName, 10), Resources = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 10)
            by UserPrincipalName, UserDisplayName
| order by LastSeen desc

id: 6f2b1c94-2e77-4a1d-9c5a-8b0d3f7e2a11

references:

logsource:
  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode
    ResultType: 0
  condition: selection
level: medium
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| stats min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("properties.ipAddress") as ipAddress values("properties.appDisplayName") as app values("properties.resourceDisplayName") as resource dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount by user
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
Kali365 concurrent device-code sign-in: same user, 2+ IPs/countries in one hour AICommand & Control Medium
Correlates successful device-code-flow sign-ins for a single user across two or more distinct IPs or countries within a one-hour window — the pattern seen when a victim approves the code from their location while the Kali365 operator uses the issued token from separate infrastructure. Adds temporal + geo divergence on top of the raw device-code signal to raise fidelity. Rationale: Builds on the article's device-code abuse by adding the operational tell that the person approving the code and the person using the resulting token are in different places — 2+ IPs/countries for the same user in a 1h device-code window. Correlation/threshold shape, so Sigma is intentionally omitted. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling user whose VPN egress and local carrier IP both appear within the hour
  • Mobile users roaming between Wi-Fi and cellular NAT pools mapped to different geos
  • Corporate proxy / cloud-egress that presents multiple regional IPs for one session
  • Legitimate CLI auth from a datacenter jump host while the user is also at their desk
  • Geo-IP database inaccuracy splitting a single ISP block across two countries
Response runbook
1. Triage: list the two+ IPs and their ASNs/geos for the flagged hour; determine which IP matches the user's known device/location and whether the other is a hosting/VPS provider (operator infra). 2. Contain: revoke refresh tokens and sessions for the account, force password reset + re-MFA, and add the non-user IP/ASN to conditional-access block. 3. Hunt: pivot on the suspicious IP across all users for device-code sign-ins, review the account's OAuth grants, inbox rules, and file/mail access since first-seen; check for token replay against Exchange/SharePoint from the same IP.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where isnotempty(AccountUpn) and AccountUpn !endswith "$"
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(Country),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(Country, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where AuthenticationDetails has "deviceCode"
| where ResultType == 0
| where isnotempty(UserPrincipalName)
| extend CountryOrRegion = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize IPs = dcount(IPAddress), Countries = dcount(CountryOrRegion),
            IPList = make_set(IPAddress, 20), CountryList = make_set(CountryOrRegion, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where IPs >= 2 or Countries >= 2   // victim approves locally, operator uses token from other infra
| order by LastSeen desc
CLOUD
sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" "properties.authenticationProtocol"="deviceCode" "properties.status.errorCode"=0
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc("properties.ipAddress") as ipCount dc("location.countryOrRegion") as countryCount values("properties.ipAddress") as ips values("location.countryOrRegion") as countries by user, _time
| where ipCount>=2 OR countryCount>=2
| sort - _time
Host or mailbox contact with Kali365 lure domains (SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign decoys) AIDelivery High
Matches endpoint web/DNS traffic and delivered email URLs against the confirmed Kali365 lure-hosting domains that impersonate SharePoint, OneDrive and DocuSign to funnel victims into the device-code flow. This is the earliest detectable stage — the lure/redirect — before any Microsoft token is issued. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the article's pre-extracted Kali365 lure domains — high fidelity because these are dedicated attacker-registered domains with no legitimate business use; catches the lure/redirect stage before a token is ever issued. Covers DNS, endpoint web egress, and mail-delivered URLs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/kali365-weaponizes-microsoft.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst detonating the lure URL in a sandbox from a corporate endpoint
  • Threat-intel enrichment / URL-scanning tooling resolving the domains for feeds
  • A previously-benign domain being sinkholed and now resolving to a research IP
  • User forwarding the phishing mail internally causing repeated URL clicks by responders
  • Newly-parked domain reuse where the string collides with an unrelated legitimate host (validate WHOIS)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the user/device that resolved or browsed the domain and whether a device-code sign-in followed within the next 30 minutes (join to UC1 signal). Confirm the domain is still live/malicious. 2. Contain: block all 20 domains at proxy/DNS/firewall and quarantine the delivering email tenant-wide; if a sign-in followed, revoke the user's tokens and force MFA reset. 3. Hunt: search email, web and DNS across the org for any of the domains, expand to newly-registered look-alike SharePoint/OneDrive/DocuSign domains on the same registrar/ASN, and push the IOCs to SIEM/TIP for retrospective search.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        where DNS.query IN ("bluefoodtruths.xyz", "flexiscalesystems.de", "guardedwebsolutions.de", "proforcstaffing.com", "reputationboosters.de", "guardextion.online", "prowebsitemakers.de", "onlinebrandinghub.de", "onsite-developments.net", "functionalityfirst.de")
